title: Authentication Fundamentals
outcome: Understand identity primitives before using a vendor: credentials, password hashing, sessions, JWTs, cookies, CSRF, expiration, renewal, and revocation.
artifact: Authentication threat/flow diagram explaining what the browser stores, what servers verify, and what happens when credentials expire.
labSteps: Draw password login without writing code and mark where plain-text password may exist temporarily.
Compare opaque sessions and JWT access tokens by state, revocation, and verification model.
Explain secure/httpOnly/sameSite cookie attributes and when browser JS should not read a token.
Trace token expiration and refresh as a state machine rather than a happy-path callback.
Separate authentication (who) from authorization (may do what) with concrete TaskFlow examples.
Write abuse cases: stolen token, CSRF, XSS, replay, brute force, user ID spoofing.
failureModes: Treating base64 JWT content as proof of authenticity
Storing long-lived secrets in localStorage by default
principles: Authentication establishes who a caller is; authorization decides what that identity may do.
Passwords, sessions, tokens, and cookies solve different parts of identity management and have different risks.
Treat credentials and tokens as secrets in transit, storage, logs, and browser code.
Design authentication flows around expiration, revocation, renewal, and failure states rather than only the happy path.

quiz.question: Which practice best matches Phase 16's engineering goal?
options: Authentication establishes who a caller is; authorization decides what that identity may do.
Move every concern into the frontend so the API stays thin.
Duplicate the same state in several places and synchronize it with effects.
Trust client-provided identity because the browser already logged in.
quiz.explanation: Authentication establishes who a caller is; authorization decides what that identity may do.
